title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We quantify the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline for intent→configuration synthesis by holding the LLM’s initial proposal fixed. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — the single LLM proposal used directly, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998); guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Under the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs McNemar convention the two-sided p = 1.00. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals; the guardrail corrected one concrete baseline failure and yielded a small measured marginal effect on the composite pass/fail metric. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks including translation of operator intent into device configuration, automated change sequencing, and limited self-repair. Operational safety in these systems depends heavily on deterministic engineering guardrails—configuration verifiers, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms—that reduce the risk that an automatically produced configuration will violate network constraints or cause outages. A common operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM produces a candidate change, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and automated or human-in-the-loop repairs are applied when violations are detected. Despite broad agreement that such guardrails matter, controlled measurements that isolate the verifier’s marginal contribution (holding the LLM proposal fixed) are rare. Practitioners therefore lack quantitative guidance about expected verifier returns in deployment regimes where the LLM already emits high-quality proposals. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment designed to measure precisely that marginal verifier+repair effect when the same initial LLM proposal is used for both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics). The scope intentionally isolates verifier-scoped safety (no high/medium-severity violations under the chosen verifier model) and a modest operational repair budget (≤1 automated repair call).
sections.related_work: Two literatures motivate and contextualize this measurement. First, deterministic network-configuration verification and analysis (header-space methods and Batfish-style analyzers) provide formal checks for reachability, isolation, and update-safety and have been shown to catch subtle misconfigurations pre-deployment [1]. Second, recent NetOps and agentic-AIOps work documents LLM-based intent translation and automated configuration generation, while emphasizing operational guardrails and multi-agent orchestration to improve reliability [2,3,4]. Generate–validate–repair (or generate–critic) patterns are widely proposed across structured-generation domains to reduce unsafe outputs and to combine probabilistic generation with deterministic checking [5]. Separate studies catalogue systemic failure modes of LLM-driven automation—hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors—and recommend verification or human oversight as practical mitigations [4]. What is less well represented in prior work is a preregistered, artifact-backed ablation that keeps the LLM’s initial proposal identical across arms and quantifies how much a deterministic verifier plus a small repair budget changes verifier-detected safety outcomes. Our study provides that narrowly scoped, reproducible measurement and situates it against the verification and agentic-NetOps literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental design. We preregistered the study (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) and fixed seeds, inclusion/exclusion rules, the estimand, and the primary analysis before execution. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where per-task success = verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations on the candidate configuration. The experiment used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task we produced a single LLM proposal that served as the baseline output and as the guarded arm’s input. The guarded arm invoked an automated single-repair attempt only when the verifier flagged a preregistered high- or medium-severity violation on that shared proposal; otherwise no repair call was made. This preserves identical initial proposals across arms and isolates the marginal effect of verification+at-most-one repair applied to the same initial candidate.

Task corpus, stratification, and modeling scope. The confirmatory corpus contained 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks generated with fixed seeds and stratified into three clusters: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), and static-route-change (166). The task generator constrained payloads to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the verifier’s modeled coverage. Tasks that referenced unmodeled features were routed to a separate cohort per the preregistration and excluded from the primary analysis; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in the run.

Model and verifier. The requested model was gpt-5-mini (hosted adapter) with single-attempt generation and a 2000-token limit. The deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) mapped concrete violation codes to severity levels and implemented a full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule. The guarded arm allowed at most one automated repair iteration, as constrained by the execution adapter.

Primary inferential procedures. The preregistered confirmatory test is the exact McNemar two-sided test implemented as an exact binomial on the discordant-pair count (n = n10 + n01) with two-sided p-value computed by doubling the smaller tail probability and truncating at 1.0. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals for the absolute paired difference used B = 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 and preserved pairing during resampling; resampling unit = task/pair. Execution accounting tracked model call counts, observed repair-stage calls, and complete-pair counts and was reconciled deterministically after the run.
sections.results:
Execution and primary outcomes. The run produced 500 complete paired episodes under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed model-call accounting: 501 hosted model calls (500 shared-initial generations + 1 repair-stage call). Aggregated per-condition results: baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency counts were n11 = 499 (both pass), n10 = 1 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 0 (both fail). Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Inferential summary and uncertainty. Under the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention the two-sided McNemar p-value for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1) is p = 1.00. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). These results reflect the preregistered tests and deterministic analysis executor; the archived analysis record contains the condition_summary, paired_contingency_table, and bootstrap parameters.

Repair-stage activity and discordant episode provenance. Exactly one repair-stage call occurred; that repair converted the single baseline failure into a guarded pass and thus created the only discordant pair (n10 = 1). The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation confirm model_calls_used = 501 and observed repair-stage calls = 1. Per-task validator diagnostics and the archived repair prompt/response for the corrected episode are included in the evidence bundle and show that the verifier signaled a preregistered medium/high-severity violation on the shared initial candidate and that a single automated repair iteration produced a verifier-acceptable candidate.

Power and sensitivity context. The preregistered power calculation targeted detection of a 10-percentage-point absolute improvement, assuming baseline failure prevalence ≈ 30% and N ≈ 384 for 80% power. The observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) was far lower than anticipated, producing a ceiling effect that greatly reduced sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. Secondary analyses by violation class were uninformative because per-class counts were near zero.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and scope. The experimental regime was deliberately narrow: a single requested model (gpt-5-mini requested), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and at most one automated repair iteration. Within that scope the LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals and the measured marginal pass-rate benefit of the verifier+single-repair was 0.002. This is an operationally framed, conditional measurement: when baseline proposal quality is very high relative to the verifier’s modeled properties, and the repair budget is small, the marginal measurable improvement on a composite pass/fail metric is correspondingly small even though deterministic guardrails can still correct rare concrete failures (one in this run).

What these results do and do not show. The study isolates one operational question—marginal verifier+repair impact under shared_initial_candidate semantics—and answers it with reproducible artifact-backed data. It does not follow that verifiers are unnecessary in general: the measured effect size depends on three interacting factors that were fixed here: (i) baseline proposal quality for the verifier-scoped properties, (ii) verifier coverage and severity mapping, and (iii) allowed repair budget and semantics. A different verifier with broader modeled properties, different severity thresholds, a larger repair budget, or a regeneration-driven guarded policy could yield larger absolute improvements. Likewise, production heterogeneity across vendor CLIs, dynamic protocol state, or adversarial intents could change baseline error prevalence and thus verifier return-on-investment.

Operational implications. First, when deploying LLM-driven NetOps, operators should measure baseline error prevalence for verifier-scoped properties on representative production workloads before provisioning repair budgets; very low baseline error rates (as observed here) imply limited marginal return from modest repair budgets on a pass/fail metric. Second, align verifier coverage with operator-critical constraints: if important properties are unmodeled by the verifier, the pass/fail metric underestimates operational risk. Third, choose generation semantics to match deployment trade-offs: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model-call overhead and preserve the original proposal for human review and repair, while verifier-guided regeneration or higher repair-iteration budgets may increase final-pass probability at the cost of more model calls and potential proposal churn.

Statistical nuance and reporting conventions. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the observed small discordant count. Small-sample exact p-values can be non-intuitive: p = 1.00 here indicates the observed discordant pattern is not statistically unusual under the null given the test convention and one discordant pair. Complementary uncertainty quantification from paired-bootstrap percentile CIs (B = 10,000, seed = 1729) yields [0.0, 0.006] for the absolute paired difference and highlights the limited precision available in a ceiling-effect regime.

Design choices and generalization. We deliberately froze design choices in the preregistration to produce a precise, reproducible answer to a single operational question. The choice to use shared_initial_candidate semantics isolates verifier+repair effect and reduces confounding from verifier-guided regeneration, but it is only one of several plausible deployment semantics. Where deployments permit regeneration or iterative human-in-the-loop repair, expected verifier impact and cost–benefit trade-offs will differ and should be measured under task/scenario-appropriate preregistrations.

Practical recommendations for future measurement. (1) Estimate baseline error prevalence on representative inputs to select study size and repair budgets that achieve desired power for operationally meaningful effect sizes. (2) Explicitly enumerate verifier-modeled properties and align severity mappings with operator priorities. (3) When feasible, complement composite pass/fail metrics with property-level false-positive/negative diagnostics and with deployment-oriented metrics (e.g., expected MTTR, rollback-safety, or canary-failure rates) to better capture operational utility of guardrails.
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is already very high for the verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, a modest verifier+repair budget may yield negligible measurable gains on a composite pass/fail metric while still correcting rare concrete failures. Practitioners should therefore measure baseline verifier-scoped error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier property coverage to operational priorities, and select generation/repair semantics that reflect deployment constraints. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of the claims above.

limitations: Synthetic deterministic task corpus limited to the verifier-modeled features; task payloads were constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, wider cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or dynamic protocol states outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — we do not claim multi-model or cross-validator generality.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) induced a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in the study evidence bundle. The run-level manifest and per-task scoring traces confirm exactly one such corrected episode in the confirmatory set.
